directions: Plant container-grown, tissue-culture-propagated specimens in rich, moisture-retentive soil in a sheltered spot with partial shade from the hottest midday sun. 'Tandarra Red' is an Australian-origin selection of the Abyssinian banana valued for holding a deeper, more stable blackish-maroon leaf color through summer heat than the more common 'Maurelii', which can green out somewhat when grown in intense sun. Like other Ensete ventricosum selections it is a single, non-suckering pseudostem that grows for several years before flowering once and dying, so keep an offset or replacement plant coming along if you want continuity. In zone 9 it is best treated as a dramatic warm-season specimen, either grown fresh from a young plant each year or given heavy mulch and hoping for resprout from the crown after a mild winter.

Set out plants after frost danger has passed in deep, fertile, evenly moist soil in full sun to light shade; this glaucous, blue-green-leaved form of the Abyssinian banana lacks the red pigmentation of 'Maurelii' but is prized in temperate display gardens for its vigor and slightly waxy, powder-blue cast to the huge paddle leaves. It has become a classic dot plant in English summer border schemes, where gardeners typically grow it as a single-season specimen or lift the corm-like base before hard frost and overwinter it indoors in barely damp sand, replanting after the following spring's last frost. Outdoors in zone 9 and warmer it can be left in place with a heavy dry mulch over the crown, though top growth is killed by any real frost and the plant depends on resprouting from the base the following season.

Plant divisions or container specimens in rich, constantly moist, well-drained soil in bright filtered light to partial shade, with protection from strong afternoon sun and wind that can shred the enormous leaves. 'Borneo Giant' is grown specifically for scale — it is among the largest plants sold for tropical garden design, producing thick, upright stems topped with leaves that can exceed four feet in length, quickly building an outsized jungle canopy in a single warm season. Feed heavily and keep the soil from drying out, since growth slows dramatically and lower leaves yellow under drought stress. In zone 8 and cooler parts of zone 9 the top growth is killed by frost, but a deep dry winter mulch over the rhizome often allows it to resprout from the base in spring; in colder climates dig and overwinter the rhizome indoors like a dahlia tuber, or grow it as a large container specimen moved under cover for winter.

Grow in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in bright filtered light or partial shade, avoiding direct midday sun that scorches the pale variegated leaf tissue. This selection produces the same bold, arrow-shaped leaves as the species but irregularly marbled and splashed with cream to white, giving a striking, less uniform effect than the solid-green giant taro; because it carries less chlorophyll it grows noticeably slower and stays more compact than the straight species, and needs slightly more shelter from wind and sun scorch. Promptly cut out any shoots that revert to solid green, since they grow more vigorously and will outcompete the variegated growth if left in place. In marginal zones the foliage is killed back by frost but the rhizome can resprout from a well-mulched crown in spring, or the rhizome can be lifted and stored indoors over winter in colder gardens.
